desc:
A marble is dropped onto the matrix at any cell of the top row. In every step it falls to the next row, landing either directly below its current cell or in one of the two cells diagonally below it (one column to the left or one column to the right, as long as that column exists).

The marble collects the value of every cell it touches, including the first and the last one. Return the smallest total it can collect on its way from the top row to the bottom row. Values may be negative.
hints: Trying every start column and every sequence of moves is exponential: there are up to three choices in each of the rows. Many routes share their ending, so look for repeated work.
Let best[r][c] be the smallest total of a fall that ends in cell (r, c). Which cells of row r - 1 can the marble have come from?

best[r][c] = matrix[r][c] + min(best[r-1][c-1], best[r-1][c], best[r-1][c+1]), ignoring neighbours outside the matrix. Row 0 is just a copy of the matrix; the answer is the minimum of the last row, and one previous row is all you need to remember.
editorial: Every fall into cell (r, c) comes from one of at most three cells in the row above, and the part of the fall before that cell has to be optimal for the cell it ends in, otherwise swapping in a cheaper prefix would improve the whole fall. So best[r][c] = matrix[r][c] + min over the existing cells among (r-1, c-1), (r-1, c) and (r-1, c+1).

The first row has no predecessors, so best[0][c] = matrix[0][c]. The marble may leave from any cell of the last row, so the answer is the minimum over that row. Each row only needs the previous one, giving O(m · n) time and O(n) extra space. Take care that the neighbour window is clamped at the borders; do not wrap around.
